Ukraine: after two nights of strikes on the power grid, Kyiv and Moscow sit down in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday

On the night of 7 November, Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones at Ukraine's energy system, according to Volodymyr Zelensky; the following night, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians, mainly in Dnipro and Kharkiv, were left without power. US, Russian and Ukrainian delegations meet in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November [1][2][4].

On the night of 7 November, a "combined" attack hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure: Volodymyr Zelensky cites 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones, and Ukraine's energy ministry reports outages in five regions and "significant damage" to electricity transmission and distribution networks [1].

The following night, 8 November, a new wave cut power to hundreds of thousands of users in the Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions; in Kharkiv, authorities speak of about 250,000 people without power, with repairs under way [2].
According to RFE/RL, more than 600,000 people are without electricity in the Dnipropetrovsk region [7].
In Zhytomyr, Zelensky reported 140 apartment buildings without heating, as temperatures hovered near freezing [2].
Zelensky accuses Russia of stepping up its strikes to "put pressure" on Kyiv ahead of the three-way negotiations (United States, Ukraine, Russia) [3].

The talks take place on 10 and 11 November in Abu Dhabi: US envoy Steve Witkoff describes "working-level" discussions on post-war security, de-escalation and the humanitarian side [5]. The Kremlin confirmed the date; Vladimir Medinsky, an adviser to Vladimir Putin, remains Russia's chief negotiator [4].
This is the fourth round of formal US-brokered talks since January 2026, and the first since they were suspended at the end of February, when the conflict with Iran broke out [4].
Key point: Moscow is striking Ukraine's power grid hours before a negotiating table, and every night of strikes weighs on what Kyiv can ask for and obtain.

The mechanism is simple: by targeting the substations and lines that distribute electricity, Russia does not just leave homes without light; it also cuts heating, water (the pumps are electric) and activity for factories and hospitals. The cold setting in makes these outages harder to bear [2].

The Atlantic Council, a US think tank, argues that Vladimir Putin is using the negotiations to buy time and win concessions, and that expectations for Abu Dhabi should stay "very modest" [6]. By contrast, the US initiative aims to make progress on post-war security and de-escalation [5].
No agreement on energy has been announced so far [4][6].
In France, this war affects you through energy prices and the cost of aid to Ukraine. An energy deal, if one came out of Abu Dhabi, would be a signal of easing for the front and for prices alike.

Hormuz: Washington extends its blockade of Iran to land borders and the Caspian, as two tankers are hit in the strait

On 7 November, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) created "Task Force Iron Gate", a cell of about 20 people tasked with cutting the land and Caspian routes through which Iran moves weapons and money. Tehran calls it "wordplay", and at least two tankers were attacked on Saturday in Hormuz [1][2][4][5].
On 7 November, the CENTCOM commander ordered the creation of Task Force Iron Gate: a staff cell of about 20 civilians and military personnel, based in Tampa, Florida [1][2].

Its mission is to coordinate US agencies to stop advanced weapons, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and what Washington calls illicit revenue from crossing Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea [1][2].
It extends the naval blockade of Iranian ports announced in July: according to CENTCOM, the blockade has prevented Iran from exporting more than $25 billion of crude oil [1][2].
Iran's military replied that the announcement was mere "wordplay"; Iranian officials say Washington cannot isolate their economy [4].

On Saturday 7 November, according to the UK agency UKMTO, a tanker was hit by an "unknown projectile" as it left the strait; the crew is safe [7]. Maritime Executive counts at least two tankers attacked that day, one of which caught fire about eight nautical miles off Khasab (Oman), tentatively identified as the Navig8 Messi, chartered by Adnoc [5].

On the diplomatic front, Qatar proposes reopening Hormuz in return for the immediate lifting of the US naval blockade and the arrival of UN inspectors in Iran [8]; Abbas Araghchi, Iran's foreign minister, says it is "time for the White House to make its own choice" and says he is ready to talk if it chooses "honest diplomacy" [6].
Key point: the United States is adding a second layer of pressure on Iran, land and the Caspian after the sea, while negotiations run through Qatar and incidents continue in the strait.

The mechanism is a vise: the blockade of ports on the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman cuts oil exports; Iron Gate targets whatever could get around it, namely the trucks, trains and ships of the Caspian, through which Iran receives weapons and equipment and brings in money. CENTCOM has not yet said what operations it will carry out [1][2].

There are critics in Washington: Joe Kent, a former counterterrorism official, sees an attempt by CENTCOM to undermine ongoing diplomacy [2]. Iraq, for its part, says the US Treasury asked it to close all its crossings with Iran except two, which would be difficult and costly for its economy [9].
Every tanker hit is a reminder that passage remains risky for Gulf oil [5][7].

The Strait of Hormuz carries a large share of the world's oil: any incident or deal there shows up in the price of a barrel, then in the price of petrol and diesel you pay in France. A resumption of strikes would push prices up; a deal on reopening would bring them down.

COP31: the climate conference opens in Antalya, with Türkiye in the chair, Australia running the negotiations and the United States absent

COP31 opens this Monday, 9 November, in Antalya, Türkiye, and runs until 20 November. The presidency is shared by compromise: Türkiye hosts, Australia leads the negotiations. War, expensive energy and the US withdrawal weigh on a conference where money for poorer countries will be the sticking point [1][2][3].
COP31, the 31st annual UN climate conference, takes place from 9 to 20 November at the Antalya Expo Center, on Türkiye's Mediterranean coast [1][5].
The presidency is shared by compromise: Türkiye hosts and presides, with its environment minister, Murat Kurum; Australia, represented by Chris Bowen, chairs the negotiations proper [2][3].
A leaders' summit is planned in Antalya on 11 and 12 November [1].
The United States of Donald Trump, which has left the Paris agreement, has sent no official representative to the conference [1].

Money is the hard point: developing countries are pressing rich countries to fund the fight against global warming more, and African countries want tripling adaptation finance on the agenda; a senior European official warned there would be "no political will" for new pledges of money [1].

The conference opens under the pressure of war: according to Reuters, fears over energy security, AI's electricity demand and US disengagement are complicating the fight against warming, and few breakthroughs are expected amid an oil shock [1][2].
Simon Stiell, the UN's climate chief, speaks of a "new world disorder" threatening cooperation; Murat Kurum announces, with Australia, a "robust" action plan in March [1][2].
Key point: a COP held in the middle of the Gulf war, without the United States, is unlikely to produce big announcements; the stake is to save the common framework and decide who pays.
Türkiye, which presides, carries the action agenda; Australia leads the final text of the formal negotiations. That text will say whether rich countries commit on money [2][3].

On energy, the oil and gas shocks push two opposite logics: speeding up solar, wind and electrification to depend less on straits like Hormuz, or relaunching extraction to secure supply; Reuters notes that fear over energy complicates the climate effort [1].

For African countries and small states, adaptation (sea walls, water, farming) is vital; yet rich countries' public money is tightening because of defense budgets and debt. That is where the outcome of the COP will be decided [1].

In France as elsewhere, the result of a COP shows mostly in the energy, transport and industry policies that follow. Here, the debate on "who pays" and on the role of energy, at a time when oil is expensive, bears directly on your heating and fuel bills.

news.2026-11-09-irak-petrole-ormuz-accor: Iraq: Baghdad says it has Washington's agreement to export its oil through Hormuz, and its sales are almost back to pre-war levels

On 8 November, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Iraq had reached an understanding with the United States to move its oil through Hormuz, via a lane near Oman. Exports rose to about 3.5 million barrels a day in October [1][3].
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Fuad Hussein said Iraq had reached "understandings" with Washington to export its oil through Hormuz, via a lane near Oman [1].

Iraqi exports rose to about 3.5 million barrels a day in October, from 2.65 million in September, according to Iraqi energy officials cited by Reuters [1]; before the war, the country sold between 3.3 and 3.5 million [3].
Fuad Hussein puts Iraq's losses from the war with Iran and export disruptions at $60 billion [2].
The US Treasury has also asked Iraq to close all its crossings with Iran except two, which would be difficult and costly [1][2].
Key point: most Iraqi crude still leaves from Basra through Hormuz; a lane agreed with Washington would give it a safer route, with no guarantee of Iran's agreement [3].

So far we only have the Iraqi minister's account: neither the terms nor the position of Washington or Tehran are known. The oil minister cites three export routes: Hormuz, Ceyhan in Türkiye and tanker trucks through Syria [3].
More Iraqi oil on the market helps calm the barrel, and so the petrol you pay for; it all depends on the strait's security.
